4: Central Park and Coal Drops Plaza transform a former rail landscape into connected public space, bringing railway traces, reused materials and planting into everyday life.
5: The site sits behind York railway station, between the historic city and surrounding neighbourhoods. The context plan locates the river, city walls and connections that inform the proposal.
6: Land use, building heights and movement are examined together to position the park within the emerging neighbourhood and connect it to the existing city.
7: A connected green and blue network
The landscape framework links parks, gardens and waterways. New routes reconnect neighbourhoods while making the station, railway museum and public spaces part of a continuous network.
8: From productive fields to railway yard
The site's history is traced through agricultural use, railway expansion and its present brownfield condition, establishing the layers that the landscape proposal reinterprets.
9: Historic field patterns, railway alignments and existing vegetation become design material. New cross-site connections and activity points turn a former barrier into a shared landscape.
10: Woodland, grassland, swales, gardens and gathering spaces are organised around retained railway traces and new pedestrian connections through the masterplan.
11: Three complementary studies coordinate circulation, sustainable drainage and habitat, and the park's interfaces with surrounding streets and development.
12: A palette drawn from the site
Orchards recall agricultural patterns, while rails, ballast gravel and crushed concrete are reinterpreted as paths, planting edges and landscape materials.
13: The plaza celebrates industrial and railway heritage through an open civic space, designed as a place to gather as well as a gateway into the wider development.
14: The plaza plan borrows the language of platforms, canopy and destinations. Clear routes, planted edges and flexible spaces connect the station, park and railway museum.
15: Dry fountains, wayfinding and signage, gathering spaces, planting and a food-and-beverage pavilion support different uses throughout the day. Linear paving and rows of trees help organise movement and provide shade.
16: The pre-concept masterplan introduces a central Green Y, connecting mixed-use districts through a public realm that combines landscape, social space and movement.
17: Site analysis examines surrounding destinations, transport access and existing districts to establish the framework for a connected urban extension.
18: Programme, building envelopes and heights are coordinated around the landscape spine, bringing offices, homes, hospitality and innovation uses into a shared urban structure.
19: The overall plan shows the relationship between building clusters, public spaces and the Green Y, setting out the masterplan's spatial organisation.
20: Park paths, themed gardens and podium landscapes extend the main spine into a more intimate network of public, semi-public and private outdoor spaces.
21: Testing the city in model form
The 1:500 physical model explores the relationship between urban massing and open space, communicating the proposal as a connected three-dimensional landscape.
22: The feasibility study transforms excavation spoil into a landmark destination, integrating indoor and outdoor activities with a distinctive new landform.
23: The project brief brings together material reuse, sports and leisure. Design principles translate the excavation resource into a public destination with a varied programme.
24: Comparative massing studies test different relationships between built programme, slopes and peaks before developing the Ridge as the preferred direction.
25: The selected option uses a sequence of rising landforms to create a recognisable silhouette while opening different opportunities for movement and activity.
26: A step-by-step massing sequence develops height, slope and programme, showing how an artificial mountain can accommodate both landscape experiences and internal uses.
27: Sports and leisure uses are distributed across the Ridge, with routes and lifts connecting activities to different elevations and gradients.
28: The circulation strategy distinguishes steeper routes for demanding activities from gentler routes for walking and micromobility, supporting a range of users.
29: Activity areas and circulation systems are coordinated across the mountain, relating each use to its spatial requirements and position within the landform.
30: A remote resort concept reinterprets the legendary lost city of Iram within a secluded salt-flat landscape surrounded by monumental dunes.
31: The idea of a rediscovered city
Research into desert settlements and the legend of Erum establishes a conceptual language of water, vegetation, monumental structures and protected landscapes.
32: One masterplan vision treats the resort as a landscape cut into the terrain, bringing hospitality spaces into a network of terraces, caves and planted courtyards.
33: The concept sequence develops rock terraces, extended caves and connections, followed by pools and planting that give the carved terrain its spatial character.
34: Plans and sections test the distribution of hotels, entertainment and support spaces within the carved landscape, connecting the concept to a functional resort programme.
35: Interior, poolside and aerial views show water and planting woven through stepped stone terraces. The landscape contrasts with the surrounding dunes and frames a sheltered resort experience.
36: The second vision reinterprets the city through a varied field of monumental columns, exploring a different relationship between built form and the desert landscape.
37: The design sequence varies column heights and their base, responds to the shape of the desert and introduces a central water landscape.
38: Plans and sections organise hospitality, entertainment and servicing within the column-based scheme, showing how programme is distributed across its distinctive vertical form.
39: Water and gardens between the columns
Perspectives reveal planted ledges, cascading water and shaded spaces within the column structures, alongside the scheme's dramatic silhouette against the desert.
40: A coastal hospitality landscape brings together arrival, pools, beachfront amenities and wellness spaces within a confidential Red Sea island masterplan.
41: Views of gardens, sports facilities, wellness arrival and dining spaces explore how planting, enclosure and outdoor amenities support different moments of a resort stay.
42: The site plan coordinates hotel keys, residences, pools, beach access and wellness facilities, connecting guest destinations with circulation and supporting infrastructure.
43: Schematic plans bring together planting, surfaces, water features, circulation, grading, drainage and services to develop a coordinated landscape design.
44: Plans, sections and perspectives develop the pool as a sequence of swimming, lounging and shaded spaces, with accessible connections and supporting guest amenities.
45: Arrival, children's facilities and wellness spaces are compared across concept and schematic stages, showing how layout and detail evolve through coordination, design compliance and value engineering.
46: The boutique hotel landscape is conceived as a terraced journey, leading guests through arrival and amenity spaces towards views of the Red Sea.
47: Curating a compact coastal hospitality landscape

The design balances the spatial requirements of the luxury hospitality brief with site constraints, including level changes, the coastal buffer and design standards, while curating a sequence of outdoor spaces between architecture and shoreline.
48: Physical models introduce a playful reimagining of Abbey Mill Pumping Station, exploring how industrial infrastructure and natural forces can support a public landscape.
49: The palimpsest study and proposed plan connect the site's industrial layers with a new landscape, using existing structures as a starting point for transformation.
50: A sequence of detailed spaces connects tunnels, water, machinery and public routes. The design curates movement through the site as an interactive learning experience.
51: The physical visitor guide brings together location, history, routes and attractions, extending the project's playful and educational approach into a usable wayfinding object.
52: A proposed conservatory reinterprets the lost warehouse wing as a living water-treatment landscape. The exploded axonometric brings together the glass roof, structural frame, elevated visitor route and planted treatment tanks.
53: From Living Machine to constructed wetland
The building section, planting studies and construction sequence develop the Living Machine, while the wetland strategy connects ecological treatment with site levels, planting and visitor access.
54: Sections coordinate inlet and outlet levels, gravel distribution, planted treatment beds, lining and ventilation. The details develop the wetland as both a working water-treatment system and part of the public landscape.
